records.title: Wounded Healers: Exploring Coping With Intimate Partner Violence Among Health Care Workers in Malaysia.
records.design: Qualitative in-depth interviews (n=6)
records.population_setting: Health care workers who were IPV survivors, tertiary hospital, Malaysia
records.key_finding: Six HCW-survivors used varied coping strategies (seeking help, spirituality, avoidance, self-harm, staying/leaving); survivors relied mainly on coworkers and sought formal help only when situations became critical, hindered by misconceptions about IPV, privacy concerns and fear of workplace gossip.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P2 (private channel makes concerns visible) / P5 (referral timeliness and accessibility) - supports the case that informal disclosure precedes formal help-seeking and that stigma/privacy fears are real barriers T-PHE's confidential channel and bounded-authority referral safeguard must address; also useful evidence base for the 'safe help-seeking' outcome domain in the FAILURE CRITERION.

records.title: Technology Access and Attitudes Toward Intimate Partner Violence: Evidence From a National Survey in Thailand.
records.design: Cross-sectional national survey, binary probit regression
records.population_setting: General population, national survey, Thailand (Muslim identity modeled as a covariate)
records.key_finding: Muslim identity, poverty, and residence in southern/central Thailand correlated with higher IPV tolerance for both genders; internet access (as distinct from device ownership) significantly reduced IPV tolerance, suggesting a role for information access in shifting attitudes.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1/P6 (coercion-recognition and informed-choice outcome domain) - complicates: documents higher IPV-tolerance attitudes correlated with Muslim identity and southern/central Thailand residence at national-survey level, which is the population-level backdrop T-PHE's coercion-recognition literacy aim addresses; supports the FAILURE CRITERION's distinction between attendance/satisfaction and actual attitude/literacy change.

records.title: Maternal victimization and neglected offspring: Child marriage, IPV and depression symptoms among Salar Muslim women.
records.design: Cross-sectional, random-effects Poisson regression (n=201)
records.population_setting: Married Salar (Turkic-Muslim minority) women, rural China
records.key_finding: Among 201 married Salar Muslim women, 65.6% reported past-year child neglect, 30.8% reported past-year IPV, and 37.6% had experienced child marriage; child marriage and IPV victimization were associated with downstream child-neglect risk.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1/P4 (decision control and STOP RULE) - supports: shows a documented pathway in a Muslim minority population from child marriage through IPV to intergenerational harm, reinforcing why T-PHE frames marriage entry as a governance threshold requiring decision control and a coercion/violence stop rule rather than treating marriage completion as automatically protective.

records.title: Child Marriage in South Asia: A Systematic Review.
records.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
records.design: Systematic review (PRISMA, 13 included studies of 520 screened), PROSPERO CRD42020190410
records.population_setting: South Asian populations (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka), including Muslim subgroups
records.key_finding: Consistent correlates of child marriage were rural residence, low education, poor economic background, low mass-media exposure and religion (Hindu and Muslim in particular countries); downstream maternal-health effects included lower antenatal care use, institutional delivery and skilled birth attendance.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P7 (repairability) / FAILURE CRITERION - supports the broader evidence base that child/early marriage clusters with reduced maternal-health-service use, relevant to why T-PHE frames reproductive-health literacy (not just knowledge/attendance) as a required outcome domain; regional (South Asia, not Southeast Asia) so context-adjacent rather than direct.

records.title: Factors influencing sexual and reproductive health of Muslim women: a systematic review.
records.design: Systematic review, narrative synthesis (59 studies, 22 countries)
records.population_setting: Muslim women, multi-country (worldwide, including Southeast/South Asian settings)
records.key_finding: Across 59 studies from 22 countries, many Muslim women had poor sexual and reproductive health (SRH) knowledge and negative attitudes shaping service access; religious and cultural beliefs, family and community were recurring barriers to contraception use and SRH service/information access.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if culture cannot override consent/safety) / FAILURE CRITERION reproductive-health-literacy domain - supports: documents the global evidence base that cultural/religious framing shapes SRH knowledge gaps in Muslim populations, which is the literacy gap T-PHE's failure criterion targets as a required outcome distinct from attendance/satisfaction.

records.title: A qualitative study on perceptions of adolescents' sexual and reproductive health education in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
records.journal: International Journal of Adolescent Medicine and Health
records.design: Qualitative (focus groups and individual interviews, feminist analytic lens), fieldwork 2016
records.population_setting: Javanese Muslim adolescents and adults, Yogyakarta, Indonesia
records.key_finding: School-based SRH education in the Javanese Muslim community was constrained by taboo and moral-panic framing around premarital sex; delivery gaps left adolescents without reliable sexuality information despite peer-counsellor programmes intended to fill this role.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P3 (cultural intelligibility vs consent/safety boundary) - complicates: shows that in a comparable Southeast Asian Muslim-majority setting, culturally cautious SRH-education framing can itself suppress the informed-choice/reproductive-literacy content T-PHE's failure criterion requires, illustrating the tension P3 explicitly flags (cultural tailoring must not override the substance of informed choice).

records.title: Intimate Partner Violence among Canadian Muslim Women.
records.design: Qualitative dominant design with supplemental quantitative data (n=8)
records.population_setting: Canadian Muslim immigrant women, 6 countries of origin
records.key_finding: Pre-migration adverse childhood experiences and family history of IPV, combined with post-migration language/social-isolation barriers and internalized patriarchal values, shaped help-seeking and the eventual decision to leave abusive relationships among 8 Muslim immigrant women.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1/P5 (decision control and referral quality: timeliness, accessibility, follow-through) - supports: documents concrete pre- and post-marriage barriers to disclosure and help-seeking in Muslim women, reinforcing why T-PHE frames accountable referral (not just availability) as a distinct success criterion from attendance/satisfaction.
records.evidence_level: Qualitative study with descriptive quantitative supplement

records.title: Muslim Women's Experiences of Domestic Violence and Abuse: A Meta-Ethnography of Global Evidence.
records.design: Meta-ethnography (33 qualitative studies synthesized), 6 databases searched
records.population_setting: Muslim women, global (multi-country qualitative evidence)
records.key_finding: Synthesis of 33 qualitative studies identified four major themes - experience/impact of abuse, risk factors, help-seeking, and coping - and found religion functions both as a risk factor for abuse and a barrier to help-seeking, and simultaneously as a coping resource for some women.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1/P3/P5 (decision control, cultural intelligibility vs safety, referral quality) - supports: the dual role of religion (barrier and resource) directly substantiates T-PHE's epistemic-humility and cultural-intelligibility safeguards, and the help-seeking/coping themes ground the FAILURE CRITERION's coercion-recognition and safe-help-seeking outcome domains in Muslim populations specifically.

records.title: Shame, Family Honor, and Dating Abuse: Lessons From an Exploratory Study of South Asian Muslims.
records.design: Exploratory qualitative study
records.population_setting: South Asian Muslim communities (diaspora)
records.key_finding: Cultural norms constructing dating as shameful were found to intensify fear of parental/community reaction and strengthen attachment to abusive partners, with direct implications for disclosure, help-seeking, and the ability to end abusive relationships.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P4 (STOP RULE) / P1 (decision control) - supports: illustrates the mechanism by which family-honor and shame norms can suppress disclosure of coercion/abuse before or during a relationship transition, which is precisely the risk the STOP RULE (pause joint work pending confidential assessment) is designed to interrupt.

records.title: Establishing a one-stop crisis center for women suffering violence in Khonkaen hospital, Thailand.
records.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
records.design: Intervention/comparison case-site description
records.population_setting: Women experiencing physical or sexual assault, Khon Kaen provincial hospital, Thailand
records.key_finding: Describes the establishment and early operation of a hospital-based One Stop Crisis Center (OSCC) for women survivors of violence in Khon Kaen, Thailand, compared against a non-intervention provincial hospital site.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P5 (referral quality: timeliness, accessibility, follow-through) - supports: this is the founding Thai literature on the OSCC model referenced by the angle brief; directly relevant to what an accountable, bounded-authority referral pathway looks like operationally in Thailand, which T-PHE's safeguards must interface with rather than replace.

records.title: [Domestic violence as a women's health issue--activities of health professionals in Thailand].
records.journal: Japanese Journal of Public Health (Nihon Koshu Eisei Zasshi)
records.design: Qualitative interview study
records.population_setting: Abused women and health/legal/community actors, Khon Kaen province, northeastern Thailand
records.key_finding: Interviews with 4 abused women and surrounding health professionals, government/legal staff and community members in Khon Kaen showed health professionals (nurses, community health workers) and, in one case, a community religious leader (a Buddhist monk) played identifiable roles in identifying, treating and supporting abused women within a multi-actor referral network.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P5 (referral quality) / safeguard: bounded authority and referral - supports: provides a concrete Thai example of a multi-actor DV-response network (health worker + community/religious figure), a template relevant to how T-PHE's referral safeguard should interface with existing Thai local response networks rather than creating a parallel pathway.

records.title: "Hitting as Light as Feathers": Religious Leaders' Voices on Domestic Violence.
records.design: Qualitative in-depth interviews (n=13 male religious leaders)
records.population_setting: Male religious leaders across multiple faith denominations, Lebanon
records.key_finding: Thirteen religious leaders reported routinely counseling on marital/familial problems and described mixed responses to DV (from minimizing rhetoric captured in the title quote to referral to legal measures), highlighting variable readiness among faith leaders to recognize and respond to DV.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Safeguard: bounded authority and referral / epistemic humility - complicates: not Southeast Asia, but directly evidences the risk T-PHE's bounded-authority safeguard is designed against - faith leaders acting as de facto first responders to DV without consistent recognition or referral practice, underscoring why joint marital counseling must not substitute for a competent safety assessment.

records.title: An empirical exploration of female child marriage determinants in Indonesia.
records.design: Cross-sectional secondary analysis, multivariate regression (nationally representative, n=6,578)
records.population_setting: Women aged 20-24, Indonesia (2012 Indonesian Demographic and Health Survey / Adolescent Reproductive Health Survey)
records.key_finding: In a nationally representative Indonesian sample, approximately 17% of women were married before age 18 and 6% before age 16; the paper notes research on child marriage in Southeast Asia specifically was scarce prior to this nationally representative multivariate analysis.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1/P4 (marriage transition as governance threshold; STOP RULE) - supports: nationally representative Southeast Asian (Indonesia) baseline data on the prevalence of marriage before the age of full decision-capacity, directly grounding T-PHE's claim that the marriage transition is a genuine governance threshold in the region the abstract targets.

records.title: Marriage is not a safe place: heterosexual marriage and HIV-related vulnerability in Indonesia.
records.design: Documentary/archival analysis and expert-informant interviews
records.population_setting: Married women, Indonesia (Muslim-majority context)
records.key_finding: Traditional practices including polygamy, early marriage and contract marriage (mut'a) were identified as enhancing married Indonesian women's likelihood of HIV acquisition within marriage, challenging the assumption that marital status is protective.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1/P6 (conventional success can coexist with failure) - supports: directly substantiates T-PHE's proposition that marriage completion is not itself evidence of a good outcome; reproductive/health-literacy and safety risks can persist or increase after marriage in a Southeast Asian Muslim-majority setting, reinforcing the FAILURE CRITERION's separation of completion from literacy/safety outcomes.

records.title: Cultural and religious determinants of HIV transmission: A qualitative study with people living with HIV in Belu and Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
records.design: Qualitative in-depth interviews (n=92: 52 women, 40 men)
records.population_setting: People living with HIV, Belu and Yogyakarta, Indonesia (Islamic and Javanese cultural context)
records.key_finding: Cultural practices (bride wealth, spousal-dispute management) and Islamic religious beliefs about husband-wife relationships, forbidden premarital sex, and condom use were reported by participants as shaping spousal sexual behaviours that contributed to HIV transmission within marriage.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P3 (cultural tailoring vs consent/safety boundary) / P6 - supports: provides Southeast Asian Muslim-context evidence that religious/cultural norms around marital sexuality can constrain safety-relevant negotiation (e.g. condom use) inside marriage, reinforcing why T-PHE requires cultural tailoring to stop short of overriding consent/safety-relevant informed choice.

records.title: Regulation of sexuality in Indonesian discourse: normative gender, criminal law and shifting strategies of control.
records.design: Historical/discourse review
records.population_setting: Indonesia, state/religious/activist discourse, 1980-2000s
records.key_finding: Traces how Indonesian state and Islamic discourse shifted from linking normative gender to heterosexual marriage toward more direct legal regulation of sexuality via criminal-code proposals, illustrating how marriage has functioned as a governance mechanism in national policy discourse.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1 (marriage as governance threshold) - supports contextually: provides historical/policy background on how marriage functions as a formal governance mechanism in a Southeast Asian Muslim-majority nation-state, background context for T-PHE's framing of the marriage transition as a governance threshold rather than a purely private event; not empirical outcome data.

records.title: Prevalence of and factors associated with female child marriage in Indonesia.
records.design: Cross-sectional, binary logistic regression (nationally representative, n=9,333)
records.population_setting: Females aged 15-20, Indonesia (2017 Indonesia Demographic and Health Survey)
records.key_finding: National prevalence of female child marriage in Indonesia was 12.53%; health insurance status and sex of household head were not significant predictors, while other socioeconomic/education factors were associated with child marriage risk.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1/P4 (governance threshold, STOP RULE) - supports: recent, nationally representative Southeast Asian baseline confirming that a meaningful proportion of marriages in the target region occur before full legal adulthood, underscoring why decision-control safeguards at the marriage-transition threshold remain a live concern rather than a historical one.

records.title: Child Marriage Acceptability Index (CMAI) as an essential indicator: an investigation in South and Central Sulawesi, Indonesia.
records.design: Cross-sectional survey, bivariate/ANOVA/logistic regression (n=1,000 households)
records.population_setting: Households, Bone District (South Sulawesi) and Palu/Sigi/Donggala (Central Sulawesi), Indonesia
records.key_finding: Household financial security, dowry practices and local legal frameworks were significantly associated with community acceptability of child marriage across two Indonesian provinces where child-marriage rates remain above the national average.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1 (governance threshold) / P3 (cultural tailoring vs safety) - supports: documents that community-level acceptability of child marriage (not just individual prevalence) persists in specific Indonesian regions, relevant evidence for why T-PHE frames the safeguard layer as needing to operate against prevailing local norms, not merely individual attitudes.

records.title: Factors affecting child marriage and contraceptive use among Rohingya girls in refugee camps.
records.journal: The Lancet Regional Health - Western Pacific
records.design: Mixed methods: cross-sectional survey (n=96) + qualitative interviews (n=18) + provider interviews (n=9)
records.population_setting: Rohingya adolescent girls (age 10-19) with experience of child marriage, Cox's Bazar refugee camp, Bangladesh
records.key_finding: Mean age at first marriage was 15.7 years; over 80% had given birth or were pregnant within two years of the survey; key drivers of child marriage included perceived physical/mental maturity norms, social norms, insecurity, and family honour.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1/P4 (governance threshold, STOP RULE) - supports: Rohingya are an ethnically Southeast/South Asian Muslim displaced population directly relevant to Thailand's regional migrant/refugee context; documents concrete decision-control failure (very early marriage age, rapid childbearing) that T-PHE's decision-control mechanism targets, though the displacement-camp setting differs from T-PHE's Thai premarital-course setting.

records.title: Girl child marriage and the social context of displacement: a qualitative comparative exploration of Syrian refugees in Jordan and Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh.
records.design: Qualitative comparative study, 8 focus group discussions (4 per country)
records.population_setting: Syrian refugees (Jordan) and Rohingya refugees (Bangladesh), fathers/mothers/adolescents
records.key_finding: In both displaced Muslim-majority populations, participants described child marriage norms reinforced across generations, with girls themselves describing having little agency in marriage decisions, alongside contextual resistance-to-change dynamics.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1 (decision control) - supports: cross-context qualitative evidence that displaced Muslim adolescent girls' agency over marriage decisions is structurally limited by family/community norms, directly relevant background for T-PHE's proposition that a governance layer is needed to add decision control beyond content delivery.

records.title: "What other option did I have?"- The effect of conflict and displacement on child marriage and early childbearing among displaced Rohingya adolescents.
records.design: Qualitative study (49 in-depth interviews, 16 focus group discussions)
records.population_setting: Forcibly Displaced Myanmar Nationals (Rohingya) aged 15-24, Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh (post-October 2016 arrivals)
records.key_finding: Participants reported perceived increases in child marriage rates post-displacement, attributed to protection fears, socioeconomic need, lost education/employment opportunity, and perceived loosening of legal-age enforcement in the camp context.
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1/P4 (governance threshold, STOP RULE) - supports: shows how a Muslim population geographically and ethnically linked to the Southeast Asian/Bay of Bengal region rationalizes early marriage as a coping response under insecurity, illustrating a real-world case where 'decision control' at the marriage threshold is most compromised precisely when safeguards are most needed.

records.title: Attitudes to and experiences of intimate partner violence among Rohingya women who married before eighteen years of age.
records.design: Cross-sectional survey, multivariable logistic regression (n=486)
records.population_setting: Rohingya refugee women, Cox's Bazar settlement, Bangladesh
records.key_finding: 61.32% of surveyed women had experienced child marriage; child marriage was associated with significantly higher odds of justifying husband-perpetrated physical abuse (AOR=2.71, 95%CI 1.78-4.11) and of experiencing IPV in the past 12 months (AOR=1.72, 95%CI 1.13-2.61).
records.relevance_to_tphe: P1/P6 (governance threshold; conventional success can coexist with failure) - supports: quantifies, in a regionally proximate Muslim population, the specific association between early/forced marriage entry and both IPV victimization and IPV-justifying attitudes, directly evidencing the coercion-recognition and safety-outcome domains named in T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION.

records.title: Women's autonomy and child survival: a comparison of Muslims and non-Muslims in four Asian countries.
records.design: Comparative study, 15 matched Muslim/non-Muslim community pairs
records.population_setting: Married women, India, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand
records.key_finding: Women's autonomy was not consistently lower in Muslim than non-Muslim communities across the four Asian countries studied (including Malaysia and Thailand), and the association between autonomy measures and child mortality was weak both across and within communities.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Complicates a simplistic reading of P1/decision-control framing - directly relevant caution: this is a rare multi-country comparative study including both Malaysia and Thailand that found Muslim women's autonomy was not uniformly lower than non-Muslim women's in the same countries, a finding that should temper any assumption that Muslim identity alone predicts lower decision control; complicates rather than simply supports the programme's implicit population framing.

gaps_noted: No PubMed-indexed evaluation study of an Islamic/faith-based premarital education or marriage-preparation course (content, uptake, or outcomes) specific to Thailand, Malaysia, or Indonesia was found; premarital-course literature retrieved was overwhelmingly about genetic/thalassaemia premarital screening, not relational or safeguarding education.

No PubMed-indexed study on secret, unregistered, or informal (nikah siri / nikah tidak dicatatkan-type) religious marriage prevalence, drivers, or consequences among Muslim populations in Thailand/Malaysia/Indonesia was located via these queries.

No PubMed-indexed study on Thailand's Deep South (Pattani/Yala/Narathiwat) Muslim population specifically addressing IPV, forced marriage, or premarital programmes was found; the Thailand-specific IPV/OSCC literature retrieved (Grisurapong 2002, Nagae 2004, Phonkacha 2026) is either general-population or historical, not Muslim-population-specific within Thailand.

No PubMed-indexed outcome evaluation of faith-leader-mediated IPV response specific to Southeast Asia was found; the two faith-leader IPV studies located in the broader search (Lebanon, Nigeria) are outside the region and were only partly incorporated (Lebanon included above as a contextual comparator; Nigeria RCT excluded from the final record set for direct-region relevance).

Evidence on Muslim populations in Malaysia and Indonesia specific to premarital decision-control, forced-marriage refusal, or STOP-RULE-type joint-versus-separated counseling protocols was not found in PubMed; most Southeast Asian Muslim marriage literature indexed in PubMed concerns child-marriage prevalence/determinants (largely Indonesia) or HIV vulnerability within marriage, not programme design or safeguarding mechanisms.

Rohingya evidence, while ethnically/religiously proximate and geographically linked to the Bay of Bengal/Southeast Asia border region, is drawn from a Bangladesh refugee-camp setting, not Thailand proper; it is included as the closest available regional Muslim-population IPV/child-marriage evidence but should not be read as directly representative of Thai Muslim or intercultural couples.
limits_of_this_search: This search is restricted to PubMed-indexed literature and PubMed's own indexing/abstracting conventions (some records, e.g. non-English-language items with an English abstract, systematic reviews, and older records, vary in abstract completeness); no WebSearch/WebFetch or non-PubMed grey literature was used, so relevant Thai-language, Malay-language, or Indonesian-language non-PubMed-indexed evaluations of premarital courses, OSCC operations, or faith-leader IPV response (which likely exist in national/ministry or NGO reports) are not captured here. Retrieval used English-language esearch queries only; the true PubMed coverage of Thai/Malay/Indonesian Muslim-population premarital and IPV literature may be under-represented by keyword choice. All 23 records were confirmed via efetch abstract text (not esummary title alone) before being described; two records (PMID 36429857, 34527969) initially appeared to lack abstracts due to an XML-parsing artifact from embedded bold-tag markup and were re-verified with full abstract text present.
